turns.text:
📚 *Learn in 2 minutes*: 5 short lessons, each with your own numbers. Write *stop* to pause and *learn* to pick it up.

📚 *1/5 · The three baskets*
Every euro lands in one of three baskets. Yours, per month over the last 3 months:
• Mandatory & regular: 1 178.18 € (55%)
• Mandatory & irregular: 151.07 € (7%)
• Slips through your fingers: 809.91 € (38%)
Plan for the first, keep a buffer for the second. The third is the only one you can change today.

📚 *2/5 · Safe to spend vs. your balance*
Your balance is 1 001.94 €, but rent of 771.82 € is due tomorrow, and usual needs and a small buffer come first. What's left, *68.60 €*, is safe to spend until payday in 9 days, about 7.62 € a day. The balance is a snapshot; safe to spend is your real budget.

📚 *3/5 · The buffer*
Basket 2, the doctor or a broken laptop, cost you 151.07 € a month on average. You can't know when, so a buffer turns those surprises into non-events. Nothing is set apart for it yet: 3 months of it, 453.21 €, would be a first buffer. S-Pankki's rule of thumb over time: 2-3 × your monthly net pay.
Source: https://www.s-pankki.fi/fi/artikkelit/nain-varaudut-yllattaviin-menoihin/

turns.user: what does pay yourself first mean
turns.text:
*Pay yourself first* means moving money to savings as soon as your salary lands, before you spend on anything else.

Usually people save whatever is left at the end of the month, and often nothing is left. If you put the savings aside first, you spend from what remains. It's like a squirrel burying a few nuts before snacking, not after the pile is gone.

Want me to check how much you could set aside safely on your next payday?
